title: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
summary: How a big C++/CUDA project goes from a git clone to a binary: the build graph, CMake's configure/generate/build phases, targets and usage requirements, parallel jobs versus RAM, and CUDA architecture lists.
outcomes: Predict which object files rebuild after editing a header, from the include graph
Explain what CMake does in configure, generate and build, and why cached settings stick
Choose PUBLIC, PRIVATE or INTERFACE for a dependency and diagnose link-order errors
Compute a lower bound on build time from total work, job count and the critical path
Pick a CUDA architecture list and predict which GPUs can load the resulting fatbin

lessons.title: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500

blocks.md:
Recall the C toolchain: the compiler turns each `.cpp` file plus everything it `#include`s (one **translation unit**) into an object file `.o`, and the linker combines object files and libraries into an executable. A large project such as PyTorch has thousands of translation units, so a full build takes a long time even on a big machine.

The naive approach, a shell script that recompiles everything, wastes almost all of that time after a one-line edit. The goal of a build system is to redo **only** the steps whose inputs changed.

To do that, the build system needs a **dependency graph**: a directed acyclic graph (DAG) whose nodes are files and whose edges say "this output is made from these inputs". Our running example is a tiny project:

- headers `tensor.h`, `log.h`, and `ops.h` (which itself includes `tensor.h`)
- sources `tensor.cpp`, `log.cpp`, `add.cpp`, `matmul.cpp`, `main.cpp`
- static libraries `libcore.a` (tensor, log) and `libops.a` (add, matmul), linked into `app`

scenes.caption: Each object file depends on its source (not drawn) and on every header it includes, directly or through another header. Libraries depend on their objects; app depends on main.o and both libraries.
Edit matmul.cpp: only matmul.o is recompiled. libops.a is re-archived and app is relinked. 1 of 5 compiles.
Edit log.h: tensor.o, log.o and main.o all include it, so 3 of 5 objects recompile. libcore.a is rebuilt, libops.a is untouched.
Edit tensor.h: it reaches add.o, matmul.o and main.o indirectly through ops.h. 4 of 5 objects recompile; only log.o survives. Widely included headers are expensive to touch.

blocks.md: How does the build tool know which headers a source file includes? It cannot read `#include` lines itself, because macros and include paths decide which files are really used. The [Ninja manual](https://ninja-build.org/manual.html) explains the trick: the compiler reports them. Compiling with `gcc -MD -MF foo.o.d` writes a small Makefile-syntax **depfile** listing every header that was opened. Ninja reads it after the compile (`deps = gcc`) and stores it in its own database, so the next build knows the exact header edges.

blocks.prompt: You have never built the project. There are no depfiles yet, so the build tool does not know any header edges. Is that a correctness problem for the first build?
blocks.reveal: No. The Ninja manual points out that a file that has never been compiled must be built anyway, and the dependencies are produced as a side effect of that compile. Afterwards, any edit to a source file (even one that changes which headers it includes) triggers a rebuild of that file, which refreshes its depfile. So the graph is always exact for the *next* build.

blocks.md: Ninja then decides what is out of date by comparing file modification times along the graph: an output is dirty if it is missing or older than one of its inputs (its [log](https://ninja-build.org/manual.html) also records the command line, so a changed compiler flag reruns the step). Make works on the same timestamp idea; Ninja is deliberately minimal and expects a generator such as CMake to write its `build.ninja` file.

Rebuild cost is decided by the include graph. Touching a header recompiles every translation unit that reaches it, directly or transitively. That is why big projects keep widely included headers small and stable.
A common misconception is that editing a `.h` file only affects the `.cpp` with the same name. The compiler pastes headers into every includer, so `tensor.h` here costs 4 recompiles, not 1.

blocks.question: In the tiny project, you edit ops.h. Which objects recompile?
options: Only add.o and matmul.o, since ops.h declares their functions
add.o, matmul.o and main.o
All 5 objects, because ops.h includes tensor.h
None until you run a clean build
blocks.explain: add.cpp, matmul.cpp and main.cpp include ops.h, so 3 of 5 objects recompile. The include edge tensor.h to ops.h points the other way: editing ops.h does not affect files that only include tensor.h, such as tensor.cpp.

blocks.question: A colleague says: "Ninja must re-scan all #include lines before every build, so a no-op build of 10,000 files is slow." What does Ninja actually do?
options: It runs the preprocessor on every file to find includes
It ignores headers and only tracks .cpp timestamps
It reuses header lists the compiler reported in earlier builds (depfiles), stored in its own database
It asks CMake to recompute header dependencies on every run
blocks.explain: With deps = gcc, Ninja reads each depfile right after the compile and saves a compact form in an internal database, so a no-op build only has to stat files, not preprocess them.

lessons.title: CMake in three phases: configure, generate, build

blocks.md: Nobody writes a 10,000-edge `build.ninja` by hand. **CMake** is a build system *generator*: you describe targets in `CMakeLists.txt`, and CMake writes the files a native build tool (Ninja, Make, Visual Studio, Xcode) executes. Every CMake build therefore has two commands: one that runs CMake, and one that runs the build tool.

blocks.code:
git clone https://github.com/example/proj && cd proj
# configure + generate into a separate build directory
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo
# build (CMake calls ninja for you)
cmake --build build -j 16
# see the exact compiler commands when something fails
cmake --build build -v
blocks.caption: The out-of-source workflow. -S names the source tree, -B the build tree (created if missing).

blocks.title: What each phase reads and writes

scenes.caption: Configure: CMake runs your CMakeLists.txt, detects the compilers, runs find_package, and records settings as cache entries in CMakeCache.txt inside the build directory.

Generate: from the configured targets CMake writes build.ninja. With CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON (Ninja and Makefile generators only) it also writes the exact compiler command for every translation unit.
Build: Ninja walks the graph and runs the compiler and linker for out-of-date steps only. CMake reruns only if a CMakeLists.txt or the cache changed, via a regeneration rule in build.ninja.
Second configure: CMake reads CMakeCache.txt first. Values you passed with -D last time are still there, even if you do not repeat them.

blocks.md:
The **cache** is the part that surprises people. Per the [cmake(1) manual](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/manual/cmake.1.html), `-D VAR=value` creates or updates a cache entry in `CMakeCache.txt`, and that entry stays for every later configure of that build tree. `-U glob` removes entries, and `--fresh` (CMake 3.24+) deletes `CMakeCache.txt` and `CMakeFiles/` and configures from scratch.

Some entries cannot be changed at all after the first configure. The docs for `CMAKE_<LANG>_COMPILER` say: once set, you can not change this variable. Switching from GCC to Clang means a new build directory (or `--fresh`).

blocks.prompt: You configured with `cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug`. Later you run `cmake -S . -B build` with no -D flags and rebuild. Which build type do you get?
blocks.reveal: Still **Debug**. The first run stored `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` in `build/CMakeCache.txt`, and the second configure read it back. To change it you must pass `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` explicitly (or start fresh). This is why "I changed nothing but the build is weird" often ends with deleting the build directory: a stale cache entry was still in effect.

blocks.md:
**Build types.** With single-configuration generators (Ninja, Makefiles) `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` picks one of the typical values Debug, Release, RelWithDebInfo or MinSizeRel. Its default is often empty, which the docs call usually not desirable. For GCC, CMake's `Modules/Compiler/GNU.cmake` initializes the per-type flags as:

- Debug: `-g`
- Release: `-O3 -DNDEBUG`
- RelWithDebInfo: `-O2 -g -DNDEBUG`
- MinSizeRel: `-Os -DNDEBUG`

`-DNDEBUG` disables `assert()`, so an assert you rely on silently vanishes in three of the four types.

Keep several build directories side by side (`build-debug`, `build-release`) from the same source tree. Each has its own cache and graph, so switching between them costs no rebuild. Point clangd or your editor at `compile_commands.json` to get the exact flags and include paths the build uses.
`cmake -S . -B build` configures and generates; `cmake --build build` runs the native tool. Settings live in `build/CMakeCache.txt` and persist until you change them, remove them, or use `--fresh`.

blocks.question: After a first configure with GCC, you run `CXX=clang++ cmake -S . -B build`. The build still uses GCC. Why?
options: CMake only reads CXX on Windows
Ninja caches the compiler path in .ninja_log
clang++ must be passed with -G
The C++ compiler was fixed in CMakeCache.txt on the first configure and cannot be changed in that build tree
blocks.explain: CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER is chosen on the first configure of a build tree (from CXX or -D) and the docs say it cannot be changed afterwards. Use a new build directory or cmake --fresh.

blocks.question: A crash only happens in your Release build, and you need a debugger with line numbers but the same optimization level class. Which build type is the best first try?
options: Debug, since it has -g
RelWithDebInfo, which keeps optimization (-O2 for GCC) and adds -g
MinSizeRel, since it keeps NDEBUG
An empty CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE
blocks.explain: Debug drops optimization (only -g) and keeps asserts on, which can hide an optimizer-dependent or NDEBUG-dependent bug. RelWithDebInfo is optimized, defines NDEBUG like Release, and keeps debug info. It is still -O2 rather than Release's -O3, so the bug may move, but it is the closest standard type.

lessons.title: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail

blocks.md: Modern CMake is organized around **targets**: things created by `add_library` and `add_executable`. A target has a *build specification* (how to compile it) and *usage requirements* (what anyone who uses it must also get: include directories, compile definitions, options, and link libraries). The [cmake-buildsystem(7)](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/manual/cmake-buildsystem.7.html) manual describes usage requirements as settings that propagate to consumers that link to the target via `target_link_libraries()`.

`target_link_libraries(T <scope> D)` takes one of three scope keywords:

- **PRIVATE**: T's implementation uses D, its headers do not. D's usage requirements apply to T only.
- **PUBLIC**: T's headers also use D (for example a class inherits from a D type). D's requirements apply to T *and* to anyone who links T.
- **INTERFACE**: only T's headers use D. Requirements go to T's consumers, not to T itself.

Mechanically, CMake reads the `INTERFACE_*` properties of dependencies (such as `INTERFACE_INCLUDE_DIRECTORIES`) and appends them to the consumer's matching properties.

blocks.title: Tracing the manual's propagation example
blocks.code:
add_library(archive archive.cpp)
target_compile_definitions(archive INTERFACE USING_ARCHIVE_LIB)

add_library(serialization serialization.cpp)
target_compile_definitions(serialization INTERFACE USING_SERIALIZATION_LIB)

add_library(archiveExtras extras.cpp)
target_link_libraries(archiveExtras PUBLIC archive)
target_link_libraries(archiveExtras PRIVATE serialization)

add_executable(consumer consumer.cpp)
target_link_libraries(consumer archiveExtras)

scenes.caption: INTERFACE definitions are for consumers only: archive itself is compiled without USING_ARCHIVE_LIB, but anything that links archive gets it.
serialization likewise offers USING_SERIALIZATION_LIB to its consumers.
archiveExtras links both, so it compiles with both definitions. The PUBLIC edge also adds archive's requirement to archiveExtras' own interface.
consumer gets only USING_ARCHIVE_LIB: archive was PUBLIC, serialization was PRIVATE, so serialization's requirement stops at archiveExtras.

blocks.md: Choosing PRIVATE for a dependency that appears in your public headers compiles fine for you and breaks for your users: their code includes your header, which includes D's header, but D's include directory never reached them. The error shows up in *their* build as a missing header.

**Finding dependencies you did not build.** `find_package(Foo)` first tries *Module mode*, a `FindFoo.cmake` script, then *Config mode*, a `FooConfig.cmake` or `foo-config.cmake` file installed by the package itself ([find_package docs](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/command/find_package.html)). Config mode searches a list of install prefixes and records where it found the file in a cache entry `Foo_DIR`. When configure says it cannot find a package you know is installed, add its prefix to `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` (PyTorch's README does exactly this for conda and venv prefixes) or set `Foo_DIR` to the folder holding the config file.

**Link order.** Static libraries add one more trap. The [GNU ld manual](https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/ld/Options.html) says the linker searches an archive only once, at the position where it appears on the command line, and pulls out only members that define a symbol that is *already* undefined. In our project `main.o` needs `add`, `matmul` and `log`; `add.o` and `matmul.o` (in libops) need `tensor` from libcore.

blocks.title: ld scanning: main.o libcore.a libops.a (wrong order)

scenes.caption: After reading main.o, three symbols are undefined (red). tensor is not needed yet (grey).
Scanning libcore.a: log is undefined, so log.o is pulled in. tensor.o is skipped because nothing needs tensor yet.
Scanning libops.a pulls add.o and matmul.o, which reference tensor. tensor is now undefined, but libcore.a has already been passed.
End of the line: undefined reference to tensor. Swapping to main.o libops.a libcore.a resolves everything in one pass.

blocks.md: If you write `target_link_libraries(ops PUBLIC core)` (or PRIVATE: a static library has no link step, so its dependencies still become link dependencies of whoever links it), CMake knows the edge ops then core and emits core after ops on every link line. The [target_link_libraries docs](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/command/target_link_libraries.html) even show CMake repeating mutually dependent static libraries (`A B A B`). Most "undefined reference" errors in CMake projects come from a missing `target_link_libraries` edge, not from wrong flags.

Declare every real dependency on the target that uses it, with the narrowest correct scope: PRIVATE if only the .cpp files use it, PUBLIC if your headers expose it, INTERFACE if only your headers do. CMake then derives include paths, definitions and link order for you.

blocks.question: Library `img` uses libpng only inside img.cpp; its public header img.h never mentions png types. Which line is right?
options: target_link_libraries(img PUBLIC PNG::PNG)
target_link_libraries(img INTERFACE PNG::PNG)
target_link_libraries(img PRIVATE PNG::PNG)
include_directories(/usr/include/libpng) at the top level
blocks.explain: Only the implementation uses libpng, so PRIVATE. PUBLIC would leak png's include paths and definitions to every consumer; INTERFACE would not give them to img.cpp itself, so img would fail to compile. A global include_directories bypasses targets entirely.

blocks.question: Configure succeeds, compile succeeds, then the link of `app` fails with: undefined reference to `tensor_new`, called from add.o in libops.a. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add target_link_libraries(ops PUBLIC core) (or PRIVATE) so core is linked after ops
Add core's include directory to app
Rebuild with -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
Delete the build directory, since the cache is stale
blocks.explain: The symbol is referenced from inside libops but defined in libcore. Without a declared ops to core edge, nothing guarantees core is searched after ops. Include paths affect compiling, not linking, and the cache is not involved.

lessons.title: Parallel builds: jobs, RAM and the critical path

blocks.md: Independent nodes of the graph can run at the same time. `cmake --build build -j N` (or the `CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL` environment variable) caps concurrent processes; if you omit N, the native tool's default is used. Ninja's default, from `GuessParallelism()` in its source, is the number of logical CPUs plus 2 (2 on a 1-CPU machine, 3 on 2 CPUs). With 16 logical CPUs that is 18 jobs; a 16-core machine with 2 hardware threads per core reports 32 and gets 34.

Worked example (a simplified model with made-up but internally consistent numbers): 8 translation units take 6, 5, 4, 4, 3, 3, 2 and 2 seconds to compile, 29 s of work in total, and then a 3 s link that must wait for all of them. Ninja hands each next ready job to the first free slot.

blocks.title: Same 8 compiles plus a link, at 1, 2 and 4 jobs

scenes.caption: -j 1: everything runs back to back. 29 s of compiling plus the 3 s link finishes at 32 s.
-j 2: compiles end at 15 s, link at 18 s. Close to half of 32, because the work splits evenly.
-j 4: compiles end at 8 s, total 11 s. The 6 s conv file plus the 3 s link already form a 9 s chain no number of jobs can shorten.

blocks.caption: W = total compile work, j = jobs, t_max = longest single compile. Example: j = 4 gives max(7.25, 6) + 3 = 10.25 s (actual 11); j = 8 gives max(3.6, 6) + 3 = 9 s, and 9 s is reached.

blocks.md: So more jobs help until the **critical path** (the longest chain of dependent steps) dominates. Past that point the remaining fix is to make the long steps shorter: split giant translation units, use precompiled headers, or a faster linker. PyTorch's [CONTRIBUTING guide](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) notes that in a tight edit loop linking dominates and recommends mold or lld via `CMAKE_LINKER_TYPE` (CMake 3.29+).

blocks.title: Peak RAM of the same schedule (8 GB machine)

scenes.caption: Give each compile a peak memory (conv 3, attn 2.5, gemm and norm 2, io and log 1.5, util and main 1 GB). Peak RAM is the largest sum over jobs running at once.
On an 8 GB machine, -j 4 needs 9.5 GB and -j 8 needs 14.5 GB. The machine starts swapping, or the out-of-memory killer can end a compiler process and the build fails with a terse "killed" message.

blocks.title: Build time lower bound versus jobs, with a RAM ceiling

scenes.caption: Simplified model: 240 core-minutes of work, a 2 minute longest compile, a 1 minute link. 8 jobs gives 31 min, 16 gives 16, 32 gives 8.5.

64 GB of RAM at 2.5 GB per job allows about 25 jobs. Ninja's default of CPUs + 2 on a 64-CPU box (66 jobs) would need about 165 GB, so the build swaps or gets killed instead of reaching the faster times the curve shows past the line.
Heavy template or CUDA files can need far more per job. At 6 GB each the same machine fits only about 10 jobs, so the RAM line, not the core count, sets the build time.

blocks.md:
Tools for the RAM ceiling:

- Pass a smaller `-j`. PyTorch's build and `torch.utils.cpp_extension` read a `MAX_JOBS` environment variable for this.
- Ninja **pools** cap one class of steps, for example "no more than 2 links at once", while compiles keep the full `-j`. CMake exposes them as the global `JOB_POOLS` property plus `CMAKE_JOB_POOL_COMPILE` / `CMAKE_JOB_POOL_LINK`. Ninja never exceeds the overall `-j`, whatever the pools say.

Tools for repeated work: **ccache** hashes the compiler, its options and the source (or preprocessed source) and replays the stored object on a hit. With CMake you enable it via `CMAKE_<LANG>_COMPILER_LAUNCHER=ccache`, including for CUDA.

"Use all the cores" is not always right. A large C++ or CUDA build can need several GB per compiler process, so the safe `-j` is roughly RAM divided by peak per-job memory, which can be far below the core count. A compiler that dies with "killed" and no error text is usually the out-of-memory killer, not a code bug.

blocks.question: In the 8-file example, going from -j 4 to -j 8 only improves the build from 11 s to 9 s. Why so little?
options: Ninja ignores -j above the number of CPUs
The longest compile (6 s) plus the link (3 s) is a 9 s critical path that more jobs cannot shorten
ccache was disabled
Linking runs once per job
blocks.explain: With 8 slots every compile starts at time 0, so compiling ends when conv ends at 6 s, and the link adds 3 s. Total work divided by jobs (29 / 8 = 3.6 s) is no longer the bottleneck.

blocks.question: A 32-core, 32 GB workstation keeps failing a CUDA build with a compiler process "killed" at random files. Each nvcc job peaks near 4 GB. What should you try first?
options: Raise -j to 64 so the build finishes before memory fills
Switch the build type to Debug
Limit parallelism to about 32 / 4 = 8 jobs (for example -j 8 or MAX_JOBS=8)
Delete CMakeCache.txt
blocks.explain: Ninja's default would run 34 jobs, about 136 GB at peak. Capping at RAM divided by per-job peak keeps the build alive. More jobs make it worse, and the cache is unrelated.

lessons.title: CUDA builds: PTX, cubins and the architecture list

blocks.md: A `.cu` file mixes host C++ with GPU device functions. Per the [nvcc documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-compiler-driver-nvcc/index.html), nvcc separates them: the device code is compiled to GPU code, the host code goes to an ordinary host compiler (GCC, Clang or MSVC), and the GPU code is embedded in the host object as a **fatbinary**. At launch, the CUDA runtime picks the image in the fatbinary that fits the GPU it is running on.

GPU code generation has **two stages**:

1. Source to **PTX**, the assembly language of a *virtual* architecture named `compute_XY`. PTX is text and describes features, not a chip.
2. PTX to a **cubin**, real machine code for one *real* architecture `sm_XY`, produced by ptxas, the PTX optimizing assembler.

X.Y is the GPU's **compute capability** (CC), for example 8.0, 8.6, 9.0, 12.0. A fatbinary can hold several cubins and several PTX versions at once.

blocks.title: One .cu file, two targets plus PTX

scenes.caption: nvcc splits kernel.cu into host code and device code. The host part becomes a normal object file compiled by your C++ compiler.
Stage 2 runs once per real target. This mirrors the docs' example --gpu-architecture=compute_80 --gpu-code=compute_80,sm_80,sm_86: one PTX pass, two cubins.
The fatbinary collects both cubins plus the PTX text (because compute_80 was also listed as a code target) and is embedded into kernel.o.

blocks.md:
Which GPUs can run that fatbinary? The [CUDA Programming Guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/01-introduction/cuda-platform.html) gives two rules:

- **Cubin**: within a major CC, a GPU whose minor version is greater than or equal to the cubin's can load it. An sm_86 cubin runs on CC 8.6 and 8.9, *not* on 8.0, and never on 9.0 (no compatibility across majors).
- **PTX**: the driver can **just-in-time (JIT) compile** PTX for any CC equal to or higher than the PTX's, for example compute_80 PTX on a CC 12.0 GPU. The cost is extra startup time (the driver can cache the result) and possibly less tuned code.

blocks.title: Fatbin contents versus GPU (2 cubin, 1 PTX JIT, 0 fails)

scenes.caption: A single sm_80 cubin covers all CC 8.x GPUs (minor 0 is the lowest) but nothing with CC 9.0 or later: those launches fail with cudaErrorNoKernelImageForDevice.
Adding compute_80 PTX keeps the fast cubin path on 8.x and lets newer GPUs JIT compile the kernel. This is the forward-compatibility insurance.
The surprise: an sm_86 cubin alone fails on a CC 8.0 GPU, because the GPU's minor version is lower than the code's. Higher is not a superset in this direction.
A typical shipping list: native cubins for the GPUs you care about, plus PTX for the newest one so future GPUs still work via JIT.

blocks.md:
**Choosing the list in CMake.** The `CUDA_ARCHITECTURES` target property (initialized from `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES`, or the `CUDAARCHS` environment variable) takes entries like `80`, `80-real` (cubin only) or `80-virtual` (PTX only). A bare `80` makes both: CMake's source turns it into `--generate-code=arch=compute_80,code=[compute_80,sm_80]`. Special values: `native` (the GPUs in this machine, CMake 3.24+), `all` and `all-major` (CMake 3.23+). The docs encourage setting it yourself because the default varies across compilers and versions.

PyTorch extensions use `TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST` instead, written as CC numbers: `"8.0;8.6+PTX"` means cubins for 8.0 and 8.6 plus PTX for 8.6.

blocks.title: Device images per CUDA file for four CMake lists

scenes.caption: Images in the fatbin (cubins + PTX). Every bare entry adds two images: 8, 5, 4 and 2. More images mean a bigger binary. The second list is 80-real;86-real;89-real;90.
Stage-1 passes per .cu file (one per distinct compute_XY): 4, 4, 2, 2. Build time grows with every architecture you add, for every CUDA file in the project.

blocks.prompt: You build with `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=80-real;90-real` (2 images) to save time, and ship it. A user runs it on a new CC 12.0 GPU. What happens?
blocks.reveal: The kernels do not launch: there is no cubin the CC 12.0 GPU can load (cubins never cross majors) and no PTX to JIT compile, so the runtime reports **no kernel image available for the device** (`cudaErrorNoKernelImageForDevice`). Adding PTX for the newest arch (`90` or `90-virtual` instead of `90-real`) would have made it work, with a JIT delay on first launch.

blocks.md: For local development, build only for your own GPU (`CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native` or a single number such as `TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST="8.6"`). PyTorch's extension docs note that the more archs are included, the slower the build, as each gets its own kernel image. Release builds can then target the full list. `nvcc --threads N` can compile several architectures of one file in parallel, and `nvcc --dryrun` lists the sub-commands nvcc would run.

Cubins run only on the same major CC with an equal or higher minor; PTX JIT compiles forward to any equal or higher CC. Ship cubins for the GPUs you target plus PTX for the newest one, and keep the list short for development builds, because every entry multiplies CUDA compile time.

blocks.question: Your fatbin contains only an sm_86 cubin. On which GPU does the kernel load directly, with no JIT?
options: CC 8.0, since 8.0 is the base of the 8.x family
CC 9.0, since newer GPUs run older code
CC 8.9, since it has the same major and a higher minor
None, since sm_86 code always needs JIT
blocks.explain: A cubin loads on GPUs with the same major CC and a minor version greater than or equal to its own, so 8.6 and 8.9 qualify. 8.0 has a lower minor; 9.0 is a different major, and without PTX nothing can be JIT compiled.

blocks.question: A CUDA-heavy project takes 90 minutes to build with CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=all. You only need to test on your own CC 8.9 GPU. Which change cuts build time the most while still running locally?
options: Set CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native (or 89)
Switch the generator from Ninja to Makefiles
Set CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=MinSizeRel
Use 89-virtual so the driver compiles at startup
blocks.explain: With all, every .cu file is compiled for every supported real architecture plus PTX; a single native target removes nearly all of that repeated device compilation. 89-virtual also builds once, but then every run JIT compiles all kernels at startup, which is slow for a large project.
